machine-learning-001.question: Which of the following supervised learning tasks is a regression task?
choices: Deciding from the body of an email whether it is spam
Identifying which digit from 0 to 9 an image of a handwritten digit shows
Predicting the price of a house from its floor area, distance to the station and so on
machine-learning-001.explanation: Supervised learning trains a model that predicts an output from an input, using pairs of inputs and correct answers (labels). When the predicted output is a continuous number, the task is called regression; when it is one of a fixed set of classes, it is called classification. A house price is a continuous number, so this is regression. Spam detection is two-class classification, and handwritten digit recognition is ten-class classification.
choiceNotes: It chooses between two classes, "spam" and "not spam", so it is classification.
It chooses among ten classes, 0 to 9, so it is classification.
Correct. It predicts a continuous number, the price, so it is regression.

machine-learning-002.question: Which of the following is an example of unsupervised learning?
choices: Dividing customers into several groups with similar buying patterns, using only their purchase histories
Predicting equipment failures from sensor values, using past records of whether failures occurred as the correct answers
Learning how to choose moves in a game so that the reward obtained by trial and error becomes large
machine-learning-002.explanation: Unsupervised learning finds groupings or structure in data that has no correct-answer labels. Typical examples are clustering, which divides similar data into groups, and dimensionality reduction, which represents data with fewer variables. Predicting with the correct answer of whether a failure occurred is supervised learning, and learning actions from rewards is reinforcement learning.
choiceNotes: Correct. This is clustering, which finds groups without using correct-answer labels, so it is unsupervised learning.
It uses correct-answer labels (whether a failure occurred), so it is supervised learning (classification).
It learns how to choose actions from rewards, so it is reinforcement learning.

machine-learning-003.question: Which of the following describes reinforcement learning?
choices: Giving a large number of input–answer pairs and learning a function that predicts the answer from the input, so that the difference between prediction and answer becomes small
An agent acts in an environment and learns a way of choosing actions (a policy) that makes the total reward it obtains large
Dividing data without correct answers into several groups so that items with similar features end up in the same group
machine-learning-003.explanation: In reinforcement learning, the learner (the agent) observes the state of the environment, chooses an action and receives a reward as a result. No correct answer is given for each action; through trial and error the agent learns a policy that maximizes the total reward received over the future. It is used for games such as Go, robot control and tuning the output of language models to match human evaluations.
choiceNotes: This describes supervised learning. In reinforcement learning, no correct answer is given for each action.
Correct. The policy is learned by trial and error, guided by rewards.
This describes clustering, a form of unsupervised learning.

machine-learning-004.question: Which of the following describes the procedure of clustering with k-means (k-means clustering)?
choices: Start with all data in one cluster and split off the data farthest from the rest one by one, dividing until there are k clusters
Place k tentative centers, assign each data point to the cluster of the nearest center and make each cluster's mean the new center, repeating until the assignments stop changing
For each point to be clustered, find the k nearest points in the training data and decide its cluster by a majority vote of their labels
machine-learning-004.explanation: k-means fixes the number of clusters k in advance and works as follows: (1) choose k centers, (2) assign each data point to the cluster of the nearest center, (3) make the mean of each cluster's data its new center, and repeat (2) and (3) until the assignments stop changing. The result depends on the initial centers and can stop at a solution that is not the best partition, so the algorithm is run several times with different initial values, or an initialization such as k-means++ is used. The value of k is not determined automatically, so it is chosen with guides such as the elbow method.
choiceNotes: This is closer to divisive hierarchical clustering, which splits the whole set step by step; it is not the k-means procedure.
Correct. Assignment and center updates are repeated until the assignments stop changing.
This is the idea of k-nearest neighbors (k-NN). k-NN is a supervised classification method that uses correct-answer labels.

machine-learning-005.question: Which of the following describes principal component analysis (PCA)?
choices: Selecting the few features that best predict the correct-answer labels and discarding all the other features to make the data smaller
Dividing data into a predetermined number of groups so that similar items fall in the same group
Finding new, mutually orthogonal axes in order, starting from the direction in which the spread (variance) of the data is largest, and representing the data with few axes
machine-learning-005.explanation: Principal component analysis is a representative dimensionality-reduction method that represents data with many variables using fewer variables while losing as little information as possible. It finds, in order, the direction of greatest variance in the data as the first principal component, the direction of greatest variance orthogonal to it as the second principal component, and so on, and represents the data with only the leading components. It is a kind of unsupervised learning that uses no correct-answer labels and is used for visualizing data and for preprocessing before training. If the variables have different units or scales, the result is pulled toward variables with large values, so the data is often standardized first.
choiceNotes: Choosing features with the labels is feature selection. PCA uses no labels and builds new axes that combine the original variables.
This describes clustering (k-means and others).
Correct. Mutually orthogonal axes (principal components) are found in order of decreasing variance.

machine-learning-006.question: When data is split into training, validation and test sets, which of the following is the main use of the validation set?
choices: Tuning hyperparameters and comparing several models
Computing the error used to update the model's weights
Being used only once at the end of development to estimate the performance of the finished model
machine-learning-006.explanation: The training set is used to determine the model's weights, and the validation set is used to tune hyperparameters such as the learning rate and the number of layers, and to compare which model to adopt. The test set is used only once, after all such tuning is finished, to estimate performance on unseen data. Tuning repeatedly while watching validation results gradually fits the model to the validation set as well, so a separately reserved test set is needed for the final evaluation.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is used for tuning hyperparameters and selecting models.
The training set is what is used to update the weights.
This is how the test set is used.

machine-learning-007.question: When 5-fold cross-validation (k-fold cross-validation with k = 5) is performed on 1000 data points, how many data points are used for each round of training?
machine-learning-007.explanation: In k-fold cross-validation, the data is divided into k groups; one is used for evaluation and the remaining k − 1 for training. This is repeated k times, rotating the evaluation group, and the average of the k evaluations is taken as the model's performance. With 5 folds each group has 1000 ÷ 5 = 200 points, so each round trains on 200 × 4 = 800 points, and training is done 5 times. Every data point is used for evaluation exactly once, so performance can be estimated stably even with little data.
choiceNotes: This is the number of points used for each evaluation.
Correct. Training uses 4 of the 5 groups, 200 × 4 = 800 points.
Training on all the data leaves no data for evaluation.

machine-learning-008.question: Which of the following is seen when overfitting is occurring?
choices: The error on the training data is small, but the error on the validation data is large
The error stays large and does not fall on either the training data or the validation data
As training proceeds, the errors on the training data and on the validation data both keep falling in the same way
machine-learning-008.explanation: Overfitting is a state in which the model memorizes fine details and noise in the training data, so its performance on new data (generalization performance) drops. A small error on the training data together with a large error on the validation data is the telltale sign. A large error even on the training data indicates underfitting, in which the model fails to capture the trend, for example because it is too simple. Remedies include adding data, simplifying the model, regularization, dropout, and early stopping, which ends training when the validation error starts to rise.
choiceNotes: Correct. The model fits the training data too closely, and its error on new data becomes large.
This is underfitting.
This shows training progressing well. With overfitting, the validation error starts to rise partway through.

machine-learning-009.question: Which of the following is correct when a model's error is considered in terms of bias and variance?
choices: A model with large bias changes its predictions greatly depending on which training data is chosen, and tends to overfit
Making a model more complex reduces both bias and variance, so it is best to use as complex a model as possible
Making a model more complex tends to reduce bias but increase variance, so a complexity that balances the two is chosen
machine-learning-009.explanation: For squared error, the expected error on new data can be decomposed into the sum of three terms: the squared bias, the variance, and the noise in the data itself. Bias is the error caused by the model being too simple to capture the true relationship, and large bias leads to underfitting. Variance is the error caused by predictions varying with the choice of training data, and large variance leads to overfitting. In general, making a model more complex lowers bias and raises variance, so a complexity that balances the two is chosen using a validation set or cross-validation.
choiceNotes: A model whose predictions change greatly with the training data and that tends to overfit is one with large variance.
In general, making a model more complex lowers bias but raises variance.
Correct. Bias and variance trade off against each other, so a complexity that balances them is chosen.

machine-learning-010.question: Which of the following correctly describes regularization and related methods for reducing overfitting?
choices: L1 regularization adds the sum of the absolute values of the weights to the loss, and tends to make some weights exactly zero
L2 regularization adds the sum of the absolute values of the weights to the loss, and strongly narrows down features by setting unneeded weights to zero
Dropout randomly disables neurons every time, in both training and inference, to give the output some variability
machine-learning-010.explanation: Regularization adds a penalty depending on the size of the weights to the loss function, keeping the weights from growing too large and the model simple. L1 regularization adds the sum of the absolute values of the weights and tends to make some weights exactly zero, so it narrows down the features used (lasso regression). L2 regularization adds the sum of the squared weights and shrinks the weights overall, but they rarely become exactly zero (ridge regression, weight decay). Dropout randomly disables neurons during training only, so that the network does not rely too much on particular neurons; at inference all neurons are used.
choiceNotes: Correct. The absolute-value penalty tends to make some weights exactly zero.
L2 regularization adds the sum of the squared weights; it shrinks the weights overall but rarely makes them exactly zero. Adding the sum of absolute values is L1 regularization.
Neurons are disabled only during training; all neurons are used at inference.

machine-learning-011.question: Which of the following steps in building a machine learning model causes data leakage (information from the evaluation data slipping into training)?
choices: Computing the mean and standard deviation for standardization from the training data only, and standardizing the validation and test data with the same values
Computing the mean and standard deviation for standardization from all the data and standardizing it, and then splitting it into training and test data
Splitting time-series data so that data before a certain date is used for training and data from that date on is used for testing
machine-learning-011.explanation: Data leakage is information that should not be available at prediction time, or information from the evaluation data, entering the training process. Computing the mean and standard deviation over all the data before splitting lets statistics of the test data reach training through preprocessing, which can make performance look better than it really is. The correct procedure is to compute preprocessing parameters from the training data only and apply those values to the validation and test data. For time-series data, a random split would mean predicting the past with future information, so the data is split in time order.
choiceNotes: This is the correct procedure for preventing leakage: preprocessing parameters are computed from the training data only.
Correct. The mean and standard deviation of the test data enter training through preprocessing.
This is the correct way to split time-series data, keeping future information out of training.

machine-learning-012.question: A two-class classification model was evaluated on 200 test samples, and its confusion matrix shows 45 true positives (TP), 5 false positives (FP), 45 false negatives (FN) and 105 true negatives (TN). Which pair of precision and recall is correct?
choices: Precision 0.50, recall 0.90
Precision 0.75, recall 0.50
Precision 0.90, recall 0.50
machine-learning-012.explanation: Precision is the fraction of items predicted positive that are actually positive: TP ÷ (TP + FP) = 45 ÷ 50 = 0.90. Recall is the fraction of actually positive items that were predicted positive: TP ÷ (TP + FN) = 45 ÷ 90 = 0.50. This model is almost always right when it says positive, but it misses half of the positives. Accuracy is (45 + 105) ÷ 200 = 0.75.
choiceNotes: Precision and recall are swapped.
0.75 is the accuracy (the fraction of all predictions that are correct), not the precision.
Correct. Precision is 45 ÷ 50 = 0.90 and recall is 45 ÷ 90 = 0.50.

machine-learning-013.question: A two-class classification model was evaluated on 200 test samples, giving TP = 20, FP = 5, FN = 30 and TN = 145. Which is closest to the F1 score?
machine-learning-013.explanation: First, precision is 20 ÷ (20 + 5) = 0.8 and recall is 20 ÷ (20 + 30) = 0.4. The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall: 2 × 0.8 × 0.4 ÷ (0.8 + 0.4) = 0.64 ÷ 1.2 ≈ 0.53. The harmonic mean is pulled toward the smaller value, so the F1 score is not high when only one of the two is high. Note that the accuracy, (20 + 145) ÷ 200 = 0.825, looks high, yet this model misses 60% of the positives.
choiceNotes: This is the recall.
This is the arithmetic mean of precision and recall, (0.8 + 0.4) ÷ 2 = 0.6. The F1 score uses the harmonic mean.

machine-learning-014.question: Which of the following correctly describes the ROC curve and AUC used to evaluate two-class classification models?
choices: A curve drawn by varying the decision threshold and plotting the true positive rate against the false positive rate; the closer the area under it (AUC) is to 1, the better the model separates positives from negatives
A curve of the accuracy at a fixed threshold plotted against the number of training passes (epochs), where AUC is the maximum of that curve and a larger value means faster training
A model with an AUC of 0.5 correctly separates positives from negatives at least half the time, so it can be considered good enough for practical use
machine-learning-014.explanation: The ROC curve is drawn by moving the threshold above which the model's output score is judged positive, plotting the false positive rate FP ÷ (FP + TN) on the horizontal axis and the true positive rate TP ÷ (TP + FN) on the vertical axis. AUC is the area under the curve, and it equals the probability that a randomly chosen positive example scores higher than a randomly chosen negative example. A model that separates the classes perfectly has an AUC of 1, and one that judges at random has 0.5. AUC compares models' ability to discriminate before a threshold is chosen, but for data with very few positives the PR curve, which plots precision against recall, can show differences more clearly.
choiceNotes: Correct. It shows the relationship between the true positive rate and the false positive rate as the threshold changes, and the closer AUC is to 1, the better the model discriminates.
A curve that shows the progress of training is a learning curve. The ROC curve shows the relationship between the true positive rate and the false positive rate as the threshold changes.
An AUC of 0.5 is the same as judging at random and means the model has no ability to discriminate.

machine-learning-015.question: For data of 1000 items of which only 10 are positive, what is the accuracy of a model that predicts every item as negative?
machine-learning-015.explanation: Predicting everything as negative gets all 990 negatives right and all 10 positives wrong, so the accuracy is 990 ÷ 1000 = 99%. On the other hand, it finds no positives at all, so its recall is 0% and it is useless when the purpose is to find positives, as in detecting disease or fraud. For data in which the class proportions are heavily skewed (imbalanced data), models are therefore evaluated not by accuracy alone but together with precision, recall, the F1 score and so on. Countermeasures include weighting errors on the minority class more heavily and sampling to balance the number of data points per class.
choiceNotes: This is the recall. No positives are found, so the recall is 0%.
This is the proportion of positives in the whole data set.

machine-learning-016.question: Four data points have actual values 3, 5, 2 and 6, and the model predicts 2, 5, 4 and 4 for them. What is the mean squared error (MSE)?
machine-learning-016.explanation: The errors (actual value − predicted value) are 1, 0, −2 and 2. The MSE is the mean of the squared errors: (1 + 0 + 4 + 4) ÷ 4 = 2.25. The mean absolute error (MAE), the mean of the absolute errors, is (1 + 0 + 2 + 2) ÷ 4 = 1.25. Because the MSE squares the errors, it is affected more strongly than the MAE by data points that are far off (outliers).
choiceNotes: This is the mean absolute error (MAE).
This is the sum of the squared errors, not divided by the number of data points, 4.

machine-learning-017.question: A straight line y = ax + b is fitted by least squares to the three data points (x, y) = (1, 3), (2, 4) and (3, 8). What is the predicted value at x = 4?
machine-learning-017.explanation: Least squares chooses a and b so that the sum of the squared differences (residuals) between the actual values and the line is as small as possible. The mean of x is 2 and the mean of y is 5, so the slope is a = Σ(x − 2)(y − 5) ÷ Σ(x − 2)² = (2 + 0 + 3) ÷ 2 = 2.5 and the intercept is b = 5 − 2.5 × 2 = 0. The predicted value at x = 4 is therefore 2.5 × 4 = 10.
choiceNotes: Correct. The regression line is y = 2.5x, so the prediction is 2.5 × 4 = 10.
This is the prediction of the line y = 2.5x + 0.5 through the first and last points, (1, 3) and (3, 8). Least squares takes the residuals of all three points into account.
This extends the line through the last two points, (2, 4) and (3, 8).

machine-learning-018.question: In logistic regression, z = 2x − 4 is passed through the sigmoid function σ(z) = 1 ÷ (1 + e^(−z)) and the result is output as the probability of being positive. What is the output when x = 2?
machine-learning-018.explanation: When x = 2, z = 2 × 2 − 4 = 0, so σ(0) = 1 ÷ (1 + e⁰) = 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5. The sigmoid function maps any real number to a value between 0 and 1, approaching 1 as z grows and 0 as z falls. Logistic regression treats this value as the probability of being positive and splits items into two classes with a threshold such as 0.5; despite "regression" in its name, it is a model for classification.
choiceNotes: This is the value of z, before it is passed through the sigmoid function.
This is the value approached when z is large enough; at z = 0 the output is 0.5.

machine-learning-019.question: A node of a decision tree holds 6 data points of class A and 4 of class B. What is the Gini impurity of this node?
machine-learning-019.explanation: Gini impurity is computed as 1 − Σp², where p is the proportion of each class. Class A has a proportion of 0.6 and class B 0.4, so the impurity is 1 − (0.36 + 0.16) = 0.48. A node with only one class has an impurity of 0, and with two classes the maximum, 0.5, occurs when they are half and half. A decision tree splits the data by choosing the feature and threshold that minimize the weighted average impurity (Gini impurity or entropy) of the child nodes after the split.
choiceNotes: This is 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.24, the two-class Gini impurity 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 without the factor of 2.
This is the proportion of the minority class, the error rate when classifying by majority vote.

machine-learning-020.question: Which of the following correctly describes the difference between bagging (random forests and the like) and boosting in ensemble learning?
choices: Bagging trains models independently on several training sets made by sampling with replacement and combines their results by averaging or majority vote, while boosting adds models one after another so that each makes up for the errors of the previous ones

Bagging adds models one at a time while emphasizing the data the previous model got wrong, while boosting trains mutually independent models in parallel on data sampled with replacement and takes a majority vote
Both bagging and boosting are methods that build one large decision tree and then cut off unneeded branches to prevent overfitting
machine-learning-020.explanation: Bagging creates slightly different training sets by drawing randomly from the original data with duplicates allowed (bootstrapping), and combines the predictions of the many models trained on them by averaging or majority vote. The models are independent, so they can be trained in parallel, and the main effect is to reduce variance. A random forest is a bagging method that also chooses the features used for splitting at random, increasing the diversity of the decision trees. Boosting adds weak models one after another so that each makes up for the errors of the models so far, and it mainly reduces bias.
choiceNotes: Correct. Bagging averages or votes over independent models, and boosting adds models in sequence to make up for errors.
The descriptions of bagging and boosting are reversed.
This describes pruning a decision tree, not ensemble learning, which combines several models.

machine-learning-021.question: The class of the 2D point (0, 0) is predicted with k-nearest neighbors. The training data consists of red points (1, 0), (3, 0) and (0, −3) and blue points (0, 2) and (−2, 1). Using Euclidean distance, which pair of predictions for k = 3 and k = 5 is correct?
choices: k = 3: red, k = 5: red
k = 3: red, k = 5: blue
k = 3: blue, k = 5: red
machine-learning-021.explanation: The distances from (0, 0) are 1 for red (1, 0), 2 for blue (0, 2), √5 ≈ 2.24 for blue (−2, 1), and 3 for both red (3, 0) and red (0, −3). For k = 3, the three nearest points are 1 red and 2 blue, so the majority vote gives blue; for k = 5, all the points are used, 3 red and 2 blue, giving red. k-nearest neighbors does no computation at training time and searches for nearby points at prediction time, and as shown here the result depends on k. Because it compares distances, standardization to align the units and scales of the features is important.
choiceNotes: For k = 3, the three nearest points are 1 red and 2 blue, so the majority vote gives blue.
The results for k = 3 and k = 5 are reversed. k = 3 gives 2 blue and 1 red, and k = 5 gives 3 red and 2 blue.
Correct. k = 3 gives blue with 2 blue and 1 red, and k = 5 gives red with 3 red and 2 blue.

machine-learning-022.question: Which of the following describes a support vector machine (SVM)?
choices: It draws the boundary so that the average distance from all points to the boundary is maximized, using all the training points as evenly as possible
Among the boundaries that separate two classes, it chooses the one that maximizes the distance (margin) to the data closest to the boundary (the support vectors)
It assumes that each feature is mutually independent within each class and classifies by computing the probability of each class with Bayes' theorem
machine-learning-022.explanation: An SVM is a classification method that chooses, among the boundaries (hyperplanes) separating two classes, the one with the largest margin. The boundary is determined only by the few data points closest to it (the support vectors) and does not change if other data points move slightly. A boundary with a large margin is considered less likely to make mistakes on new data as well. For data that cannot be separated by a straight line, the kernel method gives the same effect as separating the data in a higher-dimensional space.
choiceNotes: Only the support vectors closest to the boundary determine the boundary.
Correct. It chooses the boundary that maximizes the margin.
This describes naive Bayes classification.

machine-learning-023.question: 20% of all emails are spam. A certain word appears in 50% of spam emails and in 5% of non-spam emails. Which is closest to the probability that an email containing this word is spam?
machine-learning-023.explanation: By Bayes' theorem, P(spam | word) = P(word | spam) × P(spam) ÷ P(word). The numerator is 0.5 × 0.2 = 0.10, and the probability of containing the word is P(word) = 0.5 × 0.2 + 0.05 × 0.8 = 0.14, so the answer is 0.10 ÷ 0.14 ≈ 0.71. Naive Bayes classification performs this calculation by assuming that several words (features) are mutually independent within each class and multiplying their probabilities, and it has long been used for spam detection.
choiceNotes: This is 0.5 × 0.2 = 0.10, the probability that an email is spam and contains the word, not divided by the probability of containing the word, 0.14.
This is P(word | spam), the probability that a spam email contains the word; the condition is the reverse of the required P(spam | word).

machine-learning-024.question: Which logic function cannot be represented by a simple perceptron consisting only of input and output layers (a single neuron that outputs 0 or 1 with a threshold)?
choices: XOR
AND
OR
machine-learning-024.explanation: A simple perceptron decides its output by whether the weighted sum of its inputs exceeds a threshold, so it can only divide the input space in two with a single straight line (hyperplane). AND and OR can separate the points with output 1 from those with output 0 by a straight line, but XOR gives 1 at (0, 1) and (1, 0) and 0 at (0, 0) and (1, 1), which a single straight line cannot separate. A multilayer perceptron, with a hidden layer in between and a nonlinear activation function, can represent XOR as well.
choiceNotes: Correct. XOR cannot be separated by a single straight line (it is not linearly separable), so a simple perceptron cannot represent it.
For example, weights of 1 and 1 with a threshold of 1.5 represent AND.
For example, weights of 1 and 1 with a threshold of 0.5 represent OR.

machine-learning-025.question: In a three-class classification, the values input to the softmax function (logits) are 3, 1 and 0. About how many times the second class's output (probability) is the first class's output? Which is closest?
choices: 2 times
3 times
7.4 times
machine-learning-025.explanation: The softmax function turns each value zᵢ into exp(zᵢ) ÷ Σexp(zⱼ), giving probabilities that sum to 1. The denominator is the same for every class, so the ratio of two classes' outputs is exp(3) ÷ exp(1) = e² ≈ 7.4. The ratio of the outputs thus depends only on the difference of the logits, and a difference of 2 makes the probability about 7.4 times larger. Adding the same number to all the logits does not change the outputs.
choiceNotes: This is the difference of the logits. In the softmax function, the difference becomes a ratio through the exponential function.
This is the ratio of the logits, 3 ÷ 1, not the ratio of the softmax outputs.
Correct. exp(3) ÷ exp(1) = e² ≈ 7.4.

machine-learning-026.question: A small neural network with inputs x₁ = 1 and x₂ = 2 has two hidden neurons h₁ = ReLU(x₁ + x₂ − 1) and h₂ = ReLU(x₁ − 2x₂ + 1), and output y = 2h₁ + 3h₂ + 1. What is the value of y?
machine-learning-026.explanation: ReLU is an activation function that outputs its input unchanged when positive and 0 when the input is 0 or less. h₁ = ReLU(1 + 2 − 1) = ReLU(2) = 2 and h₂ = ReLU(1 − 4 + 1) = ReLU(−2) = 0, so y = 2 × 2 + 3 × 0 + 1 = 5. Computing layer by layer from the input to the output in this way is called the forward pass (forward propagation).
choiceNotes: This is 2 × 2 + 3 × (−2) + 1 = −1, computed with h₂ = −2 without applying ReLU.
Correct. h₁ = 2 and h₂ = 0, so y = 2 × 2 + 3 × 0 + 1 = 5.
This is 2 × 3 + 1 = 7, with h₁ = 3 and h₂ = 0 obtained by forgetting the hidden-layer biases (−1 and +1).

machine-learning-027.question: Let p be the probability that a model outputs for the correct class. Which of the following describes the cross-entropy loss −log p used to train classifiers?
choices: The closer p is to 1, the closer the loss is to 0, and as p approaches 0 the loss grows sharply
Regardless of the value of p, the loss is proportional to the square of the difference between the correct answer and the prediction
The loss is largest when p is 0.5 and becomes smaller as p approaches 0 or 1
machine-learning-027.explanation: The cross-entropy loss is −log 1 = 0 when the probability p assigned to the correct class is 1, grows as p becomes smaller, and grows without limit as p approaches 0. With the natural logarithm it is about 0.69 for p = 0.5 and about 2.3 for p = 0.1. Because it heavily penalizes confident wrong predictions, it is widely used for classification models that output probabilities through the softmax or sigmoid function. The mean squared error, which uses squared errors, is used mainly for regression, which predicts continuous values.
choiceNotes: Correct. The loss is 0 when p is 1 and grows as p approaches 0.
Using the square of the difference is the mean squared error.
The loss decreases as p increases; it is not largest at p = 0.5.

machine-learning-028.question: In gradient descent, the gradient of the loss ∂L/∂w at weight w = 2.0 is 0.5 and the learning rate is 0.1. What is the weight after one update?
machine-learning-028.explanation: Gradient descent moves the weight in the direction that decreases the loss, that is, opposite to the gradient, updating w ← w − η × ∂L/∂w (η is the learning rate). Here w = 2.0 − 0.1 × 0.5 = 1.95. A learning rate that is too large overshoots the valley of the loss and oscillates or diverges, while one that is too small makes training progress very slowly. In practice, stochastic gradient descent (SGD), which repeats updates with gradients computed on part of the data (a mini-batch), and improved versions such as Adam are used.
choiceNotes: This subtracts the gradient 0.5 directly, forgetting to multiply by the learning rate.
This adds the gradient, moving the weight in the direction that increases the loss.

machine-learning-029.question: When the derivative dy/dx of y = (2x + 1)² at x = 1 is found by the chain rule with u = 2x + 1 and y = u², which value is correct?
machine-learning-029.explanation: By the chain rule, dy/dx = (dy/du) × (du/dx). dy/du = 2u and du/dx = 2, and at x = 1, u = 3, so dy/dx = 2 × 3 × 2 = 12. Backpropagation applies this chain rule step by step from the output side toward the input side to compute efficiently the gradient of the loss with respect to the weights of every layer. Each layer multiplies the gradient received from the layer after it by its own local derivative and passes the result to the layer before it.
choiceNotes: This finds only dy/du = 2u = 6 and forgets to multiply by du/dx = 2.
This is the value of y at x = 1, 3² = 9, not the derivative.

machine-learning-030.question: In a neural network with many stacked layers, which of the following is the reason that using the sigmoid function as the activation function makes the layers near the input hard to train?
choices: The derivative of the sigmoid function is at most 0.25, so the gradient shrinks each time it passes through a layer in backpropagation and becomes almost 0 in the layers near the input
The output of the sigmoid function is not confined to the range 0 to 1, so values grow at each layer and the computation overflows
The sigmoid function has points where it cannot be differentiated, so some layers cannot obtain gradients in backpropagation
machine-learning-030.explanation: In backpropagation, the derivatives of the activation functions of successive layers are multiplied into the gradient one after another. The derivative of the sigmoid function, σ(z)(1 − σ(z)), is at most 0.25, so after 10 layers, for example, the gradient becomes as small as 0.25¹⁰ ≈ 9.5 × 10⁻⁷. This is called the vanishing gradient problem. Countermeasures include using ReLU, whose derivative is 1 over the positive range, adding residual (skip) connections that carry signals past layers, choosing the initial weights carefully, and using batch normalization.
choiceNotes: Correct. The repeated multiplication by derivatives smaller than 1 makes the gradient vanish.
The output of the sigmoid function is confined to the range 0 to 1, so values do not overflow.
The sigmoid function can be differentiated everywhere.

machine-learning-031.question: A model is trained on 10,000 training samples with a mini-batch size (batch size) of 50. How many weight updates are there in one epoch?
machine-learning-031.explanation: An epoch is the unit of training in which the entire training set has been used once. In mini-batch training, the gradient is computed for each mini-batch and the weights are updated once, so the number of updates per epoch (the number of iterations) is 10000 ÷ 50 = 200. Training for 10 epochs makes 2000 updates in total. Mini-batch training lies between batch training, which updates once using all the data, and online training, which updates after every single sample.
choiceNotes: This is the batch size, the number of samples used in one update.
This is the total number of updates after 10 epochs of training.

machine-learning-032.question: How many trainable parameters does a fully connected layer with 64 inputs and 32 outputs (one bias per output) have?
machine-learning-032.explanation: A fully connected layer has one weight for every pair of an input and an output, so there are 64 × 32 = 2048 weights. Adding the 32 biases, one per output, gives 2048 + 32 = 2080 parameters. In general, a fully connected layer with n inputs and m outputs has (n + 1) × m parameters. A convolutional layer reuses the same filter over the whole image, so it has far fewer parameters than a fully connected layer for an input of the same size.
choiceNotes: This is the sum of the numbers of inputs and outputs. There is a weight for every input–output pair, so the numbers are multiplied.
This forgets to count the 32 biases.

machine-learning-033.question: A 28×28 single-channel image is convolved with a 5×5 filter (stride 1, no padding), followed by 2×2 max pooling (stride 2). What are the height and width of the output?
machine-learning-033.explanation: The output size of a convolution is (N + 2P − F) ÷ S + 1, where N is the input size, F the filter size, P the padding and S the stride. (28 + 0 − 5) ÷ 1 + 1 = 24, so the output after convolution is 24×24. 2×2 max pooling with stride 2 keeps one maximum for each 2×2 region, halving the height and width to 12×12. Pooling has no trainable parameters; it shrinks the data to reduce computation and makes the network less sensitive to small shifts in position.
choiceNotes: Correct. Convolution gives 24×24 and pooling gives 12×12.
This skips the convolution and applies pooling directly to the 28×28 image.
This is the size after convolution, without pooling.

machine-learning-034.question: Which of the following correctly describes recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and LSTMs?
choices: An RNN applies the same filter at every position of an image to extract local features, and an LSTM improves its pooling layer to make it robust to shifts in position
An RNN treats all elements of a sequence independently and processes them simultaneously in parallel without using results from earlier time steps, so longer sequences train faster

An RNN processes a sequence in order, carrying the hidden state from one time step to the next, and an LSTM uses gates to control whether information is kept or forgotten, making vanishing gradients less likely on long sequences
machine-learning-034.explanation: An RNN processes sequence data such as text, audio or sensor time series one element at a time, passing the information so far to the next time step as a hidden state. Because errors are propagated back through time, gradients readily vanish or explode on long sequences, making it hard to learn information from the distant past. An LSTM has a cell that stores information and input, forget and output gates, so it can keep needed information for a long time. However, both must compute in time order and are hard to parallelize, and the Transformer improved on this point.
choiceNotes: This describes a convolutional neural network (CNN).
An RNN uses the result of the previous time step, so it must compute in time order and is hard to parallelize along the sequence.
Correct. It processes the sequence by carrying the hidden state forward, and the LSTM's gates make long-range dependencies easier to handle.

machine-learning-035.question: Which of the following describes the self-attention used in the Transformer?
choices: It reads the elements of a sequence one at a time from the beginning and combines the information of the whole sequence by passing each element's hidden state to the next element

It computes weights from the similarity between each token's query and the keys of all tokens and takes the weighted sum of the values, so the computation for all positions of the sequence can be done in parallel
For each token it stacks many layers of convolutions that look only at a fixed number of neighboring tokens, so that relationships with distant tokens are not handled
machine-learning-035.explanation: In self-attention, a query (Q), key (K) and value (V) are made from each token's vector, the dot products of a query with all keys are turned into weights by the softmax function, and the weighted sum of the values is computed. Every token can take in information from distant tokens directly, and because the computation can be expressed as matrix products and does not need to wait for the result of the previous time step as in an RNN, all positions of the sequence can be computed in parallel during training. The computation itself contains no word-order information, so it is combined with positional encoding, which adds position information. On the other hand, the amount of computation grows with the square of the sequence length.
choiceNotes: This is how an RNN processes a sequence. It computes in time order, so it is hard to parallelize.
Correct. The relationships between all pairs of tokens are obtained as weights and computed in parallel with matrix products.
Self-attention can directly handle relationships with every token in the sequence, not just nearby ones.

machine-learning-036.question: Which of the following describes transfer learning, in which a model trained on a large amount of data is used for a different task with little data?
choices: Starting from the weights of the trained model, the output layer is replaced to suit the new task, or part or all of the model is retrained on the new data (fine-tuning)
The trained model is not used; all layers are retrained from randomly initialized weights using only the small amount of data for the new task
A small model is trained to imitate the outputs of a large model so that the same task can be solved with less computation and memory
machine-learning-036.explanation: Transfer learning applies the features that a model learned on one task to a different task. For example, the layers near the input of a CNN trained on a large number of images can extract general features such as edges and textures, so only the output layer is replaced and trained for the new task, or the whole network is retrained with a small learning rate (fine-tuning). It tends to reach high performance with less data and computation than training from scratch, and it is also used to adapt language models to specific uses.
choiceNotes: Correct. The trained weights are the starting point and are retrained to suit the new task.
This trains from scratch and does not make use of the features the trained model acquired.
This describes knowledge distillation, a method for making a model for the same task smaller.

machine-learning-037.question: Which of the following correctly describes models that generate images and similar data?
choices: A GAN (generative adversarial network) trains only the discriminator, which tells real data from fakes, and does not train the generator, which produces the data
A diffusion model produces an image by performing the noise-removal computation only once, so it needs less computation to generate than a GAN
A diffusion model considers a process that adds noise to data little by little, learns to remove that noise step by step, and generates images from noise
machine-learning-037.explanation: A GAN trains two networks alternately so that they compete with each other: a generator that produces data and a discriminator that judges whether data is real or made by the generator. A diffusion model learns a network that estimates and removes the noise at each step, so as to reverse the process of adding noise to data little by little, and generates data step by step from pure noise. A diffusion model needs computation over many steps to generate, but its training tends to be stable and it can produce diverse, high-quality images.
choiceNotes: A GAN trains both the generator and the discriminator, alternately.
A diffusion model repeats the noise-removal computation over many steps, so generation generally needs more computation than with a GAN.
Correct. It learns to remove noise step by step and produces data from noise.

machine-learning-038.question: Which of the following describes how a large language model (LLM) processes text?
choices: It converts text into character codes one character at a time, treats characters with close code values as close in meaning, and predicts the next character
It splits text into tokens (units such as words or parts of words), converts each token into an embedding vector for processing, and predicts the probability of the next token
It replaces every word in the text with a dictionary headword before processing, so it cannot process text containing words or new expressions not in the dictionary
machine-learning-038.explanation: An LLM handles text by splitting it into units called tokens. A token is not necessarily a whole word: frequent words become a single token and rare words are split into several pieces, so words not in any dictionary can still be handled. Each token is converted into an embedding vector obtained through training, and tokens with similar meanings or usage end up with similar vectors. The model predicts the probability of the next token from the tokens so far and generates text by repeatedly appending the chosen token.
choiceNotes: The size of a character code has nothing to do with meaning, so embedding vectors obtained through training are used instead.
Correct. It splits text into tokens, turns them into embedding vectors and predicts the next token.
Words can be split into tokens such as parts of words, so words not in the dictionary can be handled.

machine-learning-039.question: When building a model that predicts hiring decisions from application documents, using past hiring outcomes as the correct answers, which of the following should be kept in mind?
choices: If past decisions were biased by gender or other factors, the model may learn that bias and reproduce or amplify it
If there is enough data, the biases in the original data cancel out, so the model's predictions naturally become fair
If the gender column is removed from the input beforehand, bias cannot enter the model through other features
machine-learning-039.explanation: A machine learning model learns the tendencies in its training data as they are, so it also learns biases in the data, such as discrimination contained in past decisions or a shortage of data for particular groups. Adding more biased data does not remove the bias itself, and even with the gender column removed, bias can remain through features closely related to it, such as career history or hobbies. It is important to review how the data was collected, check error rates for each group and evaluate fairness.
choiceNotes: Correct. The model can learn the bias in the data and reproduce it as is.
However much biased data is added, the bias does not disappear.
Bias can remain through other features closely related to gender (proxy variables).

machine-learning-040.question: Which of the following describes explainable AI (XAI)?
choices: Publishing the number of parameters and layers of a model to inform users of its size and structure
Adding training data or enlarging the model to make prediction accuracy as high as possible
Techniques and ideas for showing, in a form people can understand, why a model made a given prediction and which features influenced it
machine-learning-040.explanation: Complex models such as deep learning models tend to become black boxes: even when they perform well, it is hard to see why they made a given prediction. XAI is the set of techniques and ideas that let people check the reasons for predictions, using methods that compute each feature's contribution to a prediction (such as SHAP and LIME) or heat maps that show which part of an image influenced the decision. It helps in fields that require decisions to be explained, such as medicine and lending, and in finding errors and biases in models.
choiceNotes: The number of parameters and the structure only describe the model's size; they do not explain individual predictions.
Improving performance and being able to explain the reasons for predictions are separate issues.
Correct. It shows the reasons for predictions in a form people can understand.
